claims.statement: BidPoint is an organization-level monorepo in early scaffolding: its documentation establishes intended architecture and module boundaries, while almost all application, infrastructure, deployment, and test implementation is still absent.

AGENTS.md is the authoritative agent guide, agents must read an affected module's README before changing it, and OpenWiki is optional just-in-time context rather than a replacement for authoritative source and tests.

Every committed artifact has exactly one owning module; a change may coordinate multiple modules only when the pull request identifies the affected owners and explains why the coordination is necessary.

Repository ownership is divided among backend server behavior, independent frontend clients, backend runtime configuration, Kubernetes desired state, cloud infrastructure, automation, and durable engineering knowledge rather than being shared merely because all artifacts live in one monorepo.

The backend is intended to own authoritative business rules and APIs, while web and mobile are independent client workspaces that must not import each other's implementation and may share material only through independent versioned packages or common API contracts.

A backend application behavior setting belongs to config, a Kubernetes operating control belongs to gitops, and a cloud foundation resource belongs to infra; ownership is determined by the semantic reader rather than file format or environment-variable representation.

A backend workload manifest may set only SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME, and SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT plus secret-backed variables; another backend behavior variable creates duplicate ownership and can silently override config-delivered values through Spring Boot binding and precedence.

Mobile build, signing, and store-release configuration remains owned by the mobile workspace because it is inseparable from that client toolchain, while the automation that executes it belongs under .github.

Secret values must never be committed: passwords, tokens, API keys, and credential-bearing connection strings live in AWS Secrets Manager or Vault, while Git may contain only infrastructure declarations for secret-manager resources and workload references to externally resolved values.

Frontend settings are client-owned but must remain non-sensitive because browser output, mobile bundles, and device traffic are inspectable by users; the backend-only root config module is not a frontend configuration source.
The root ignore rules exclude .env and .env.* while allowing .env.example, which is only a guard against common accidental commits and does not relax the repository-wide prohibition on secret values.

The exact environment model is local, dev, stage, and prod: local is developer-machine execution outside repository-declared Kubernetes and cloud infrastructure, while dev, stage, and prod are isolated remote Kubernetes environments; a change for one must not implicitly alter another, and backend source receives environment knowledge at runtime rather than hardcoding it.

Agents must not silently invent an unresolved architecture decision; significant accepted choices belong in docs/adr with context and rejected alternatives, and superseded ADRs are retained as superseded rather than deleted.

The repository requires narrowly scoped changes and path-aware future automation, so unrelated modules should not be rebuilt or validated and repeated cross-domain workflow dependencies are treated as evidence that a boundary may be wrong.

Current review governance consists of one wildcard CODEOWNERS route to a default owner plus a pull request checklist for ownership, cross-module coordination, secrets, responsibility changes, and ADRs; per-module ownership rules are not implemented.

The concrete OpenWiki workflow runs on manual dispatch or a daily schedule, checks out full history, installs pinned OpenWiki and Mermaid tooling on Node 22, executes openwiki code --update --print, and opens a reviewable update pull request limited to selected documentation and agent-guidance paths.

The OpenWiki updater uses write permissions and secret references for its documentation-update operation, but it is not evidence of a BidPoint product build, test, infrastructure apply, GitOps validation, or deployment pipeline.

The intended delivery contract separates artifact publication from cluster deployment: CI builds and publishes artifacts, desired image state is changed in gitops, and a GitOps controller reconciles Kubernetes; CI may deliver non-cluster artifacts directly but must not deploy cluster workloads itself.

No current product-wide build or test command is defined because backend services, client toolchains, configuration sets, Kubernetes workload trees, infrastructure code, and concrete product workflows have not yet been implemented; agents must use the narrowest validation the owning module actually supports and preserve complete failure output.
Agents must treat old/ as nonexistent and never read, search, cite, or edit it.

Backend behavior settings are intended to be served to Spring Boot services by a configuration server, with Spring Cloud Config expected, but no configuration sets or server exist and the local delivery mechanism remains undecided.

An integration that requires a shared credential cannot put that credential in web or mobile configuration; users can inspect client artifacts and traffic, so credential-bearing provider integration belongs behind a server-side boundary.
